title: Quantitative Aptitude Questions for CAT: Syllabus, Topic Weights & How to Score + Free Quiz

meta_desc: Master Quantitative Aptitude questions for CAT: the QA syllabus, which topics carry weight, how to build accuracy and speed, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: The CAT quant section is not vast — it just looks that way. Here is the QA syllabus that actually matters, the topics that carry the marks, and how to build the accuracy and speed a 99 percentile needs, with a free eight-question quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
The single most common mistake I see in CAT preparation is aspirants treating Quantitative Aptitude questions for CAT like a school syllabus to be finished cover to cover. They buy a thousand-page book, start at chapter one, and burn two months on topics that the exam barely touches. The QA section only carries 22 questions in 40 minutes — it rewards depth in a handful of high-frequency areas far more than shallow coverage of everything. If you know which questions actually turn up and how to attack them under a clock, quant becomes the most scorable of the three sections.

This guide breaks down the real CAT quant syllabus, the topics that carry the most weight, how to build accuracy before speed, the mock discipline that makes it stick, and the traps that quietly cost good candidates ten marks a paper.

What quantitative aptitude questions for CAT actually test

Quantitative Aptitude is the third and final section of the CAT, and by the time you reach it your brain is already 80 minutes tired — something most study plans ignore. You get 40 minutes for roughly 22 questions. Some are standard MCQs carrying +3 for a correct answer and −1 for a wrong one; the rest are TITA (Type In The Answer), which have no negative marking. That TITA detail changes everything: on a TITA question you should always type your best value, because a blank and a wrong answer cost exactly the same — nothing.

The questions are not about advanced mathematics. Almost all of them sit at a strong Class 10 level, dressed up in wordy, deliberately confusing language. The difficulty is rarely the maths; it is reading the problem correctly and choosing an efficient method fast.

The five areas of the CAT quant syllabus

Quantitative Aptitude questions for CAT fall into five broad buckets. They are not equally important, and pretending they are is how aspirants waste time.

AreaWhat it coversRough share of QA
ArithmeticPercentages, ratio & proportion, averages, time-speed-distance, time & work, profit-loss, mixtures, simple & compound interestHighest — often 40–50%
AlgebraLinear & quadratic equations, functions, inequalities, logarithms, surds, maxima-minimaMedium–High
Number systemsFactors, remainders, divisibility, base changes, HCF-LCM, last-digit cyclesMedium
Geometry & mensurationTriangles, circles, polygons, coordinate geometry, 2D & 3D areas and volumesMedium
Modern mathsPermutations & combinations, probability, set theory, progressionsLowest — a few questions

Where to spend your first three months

Arithmetic. Every year, arithmetic quietly dominates the QA section, and it hides inside problems that look like they belong to other areas. A question that reads like algebra often collapses into a simple ratio once you set it up. In my experience, an aspirant with automatic arithmetic and average algebra clears the QA sectional cut-off comfortably; the reverse rarely holds. Fix percentages, ratios and time-speed-distance until you can do them without a scratch pad, then layer everything else on top.

Accuracy first, speed second — never the reverse

The instinct is to chase speed. That is backwards. A candidate who attempts 18 questions at 60% accuracy scores worse, after negatives, than one who attempts 13 at 90%. Selection and accuracy beat raw volume in a section with negative marking.

So for the first phase, forget the timer. Solve questions untimed, write every step, and after each one ask two things: was my method the shortest available, and did I read every word of the question? Only once your untimed accuracy crosses about 85% on a topic do you start timing it. Speed then comes from three habits, not from rushing:

  • Approximation. CAT options are usually spread far enough apart that a 5% estimate picks the right one. Learn to round early — treat ₹1,97,600 as roughly two lakh and refine only if the options are close.
  • Option elimination. Plug the answer choices back into the problem instead of solving forward. On many quant questions, testing the middle option and adjusting is faster than the ‘proper’ algebra.
  • Mental calculation. Memorise squares to 30, cubes to 15, fraction-to-percentage conversions and the common Pythagorean triples. These shave seconds off dozens of questions and add up to whole extra attempts.

Mock and practice discipline for quant

Practising Quantitative Aptitude questions for CAT is not the same as solving them. The score is almost irrelevant; the review is where percentile is built. After every sectional or mock, sort each quant question into four buckets: correct and fast, correct but slow, wrong, and skipped. The ‘correct but slow’ pile is the one to obsess over — those are marks you already have but cannot afford at 40 minutes for 22 questions.

Keep a running error log across papers. After five or six analysed sets, patterns surface: maybe you always misread ‘at least’ as ‘exactly’, or you keep attempting the one geometry question that eats four minutes. That log, not your raw scores, is what moves the needle. One honest caveat — do not do a mock a day. Two well-analysed mocks a week beat seven rushed ones, because analysis is slower than solving and far more valuable.

Common traps in CAT quant questions

Most wrong answers in QA are not maths errors; they are trap errors. The examiner plants the wrong option deliberately.

  • The successive-percentage trap. A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall is not zero — it is a 4% net loss. The ‘0%’ option is always sitting there.
  • Units and rounding. Speed given in km/h, distance in metres, time in seconds. Half the time-speed-distance mistakes are unit slips, not method slips.
  • The ‘how many more’ misread. Questions ask for the difference, and the tempting option is the total. Read the final line twice.
  • Ratio without a common base. Averaging two ratios directly is wrong; you must return to actual quantities first.

quiz.title: CAT Quantitative Aptitude Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight CAT-level quant questions across arithmetic, algebra, number systems, geometry and modern maths. Attempt each under a soft timer, then press Check my score and read every explanation.
quiz.about: CAT Quantitative Aptitude across all five syllabus areas

questions.q: The unit digit of 7 raised to the power 95 is:
questions.explanation: The unit digit of powers of 7 cycles 7, 9, 3, 1 with period 4. Since 95 leaves remainder 3 on division by 4, the unit digit is the third in the cycle, which is 3.

questions.q: If the price of sugar rises by 25%, by what percent must a family cut consumption to keep its total sugar spend unchanged?
questions.explanation: A 25% rise means the new price is 5/4 of the old. To keep spend fixed, consumption must fall to 4/5, a drop of 1/5, which is 20%.

questions.q: A car covers the first half of a distance at 40 km/h and the second half at 60 km/h. Its average speed for the whole trip is:
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average speed is the harmonic mean: (2 × 40 × 60) ÷ (40 + 60) = 4800 ÷ 100 = 48 km/h. It is not the simple average of 50.

questions.q: The difference between compound interest and simple interest on ₹5,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years is:
questions.explanation: SI = 5000 × 10% × 2 = ₹1,000. CI = 5000 × (1.1² − 1) = ₹1,050. The difference is ₹50, which equals interest on the first year’s interest.

questions.q: If a + b = 7 and ab = 12, then a² + b² equals:
A circle is inscribed in a square of side 14 cm. Taking π = 22/7, the area of the circle is:
questions.explanation: The circle’s diameter equals the square’s side, so radius = 7 cm. Area = (22/7) × 7 × 7 = 154 cm².

questions.q: In how many ways can 3 boys and 2 girls sit in a row so that the two girls are always together?
questions.explanation: Tie the two girls into one block, giving 4 units to arrange: 4! = 24 ways. The girls can swap within the block in 2! = 2 ways. Total = 24 × 2 = 48.

questions.q: A number is chosen at random from 1 to 20. The probability that it is a multiple of 3 is:
questions.explanation: The multiples of 3 up to 20 are 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 and 18 — six numbers. The probability is 6/20 = 3/10.

faq.q: What is the syllabus for Quantitative Aptitude in CAT?
faq.a: QA spans five areas — arithmetic (percentages, ratio, time-speed-distance, profit-loss, interest), algebra (equations, functions, inequalities), number systems (remainders, factors, divisibility), geometry & mensuration, and modern maths (permutations, combinations, probability, progressions). The mathematics sits around a strong Class 10 level; the challenge is wording and time.

faq.q: How many questions are in the CAT quant section?
faq.a: Recent papers carry about 22 Quantitative Aptitude questions in a 40-minute section. A mix of MCQs (with −1 negative marking) and TITA questions (no negative marking) — so always attempt every TITA, because a blank and a wrong answer cost the same there.

faq.q: Which quant topics carry the most weight in CAT?
faq.a: Arithmetic, by a distance — percentages, ratios, averages, time-speed-distance and profit-loss appear most often and reward accuracy. Build those to automatic before pouring weeks into probability or permutations, which contribute only a handful of questions.

faq.q: How do I improve speed in CAT quant without losing accuracy?
faq.a: Fix accuracy first, untimed, until you clear about 85% on a topic. Then speed comes from approximation, plugging answer options back into the problem, and memorising squares, cubes and fraction-percentage conversions — not from rushing, which just multiplies negative marks.
